metadata.title: Understanding Students’ Subjective and Eudaimonic Well-Being: Combining both Machine Learning and Classical Statistics

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses publicly available PISA 2018 Hong Kong microdata (6,037 students) and constructs composite well-being scales and predictor indices using OECD’s item response modelling. The manuscript does not report whether complex survey sampling weights or replicate weights were applied in the random forest and subsequent hierarchical linear modelling, nor does it name any PISA weight variables. Because the analysis combines ML (random forest regression) with HLM to account for nesting (students within schools), the authors appear to focus on structural dependence rather than explicit survey-weighted population inference. Given the absence of explicit weight handling, the results should be interpreted as model-based associations for the analyzed sample rather than fully design-weighted estimates of population parameters.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values handling is not applicable because the dependent variables are non-cognitive well-being constructs measured via Likert-scale items (positive affect, negative affect, life satisfaction, and meaning in life) rather than PV-based cognitive achievement scores. Missing data handling is reported: the authors imputed missing values using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), which is consistent with multiple imputation. Therefore, PV-specific procedures are not required for the modeled outcomes.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the publicly available PISA 2018 Hong Kong dataset. The analytic sample consists of 6,037 adolescents from Hong Kong, China (mean age 15.73), with grade distribution reported (mostly grade 10 and grade 9). The study selected 29 predictor variables from the PISA student questionnaire and retained ESCS while excluding other SES components to avoid multicollinearity. Missing data were imputed using MCMC prior to standardization and model fitting; no additional task- or module-based exclusions are described.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest regression with 10-fold cross-validation (5 repeats): R² = 19.15%, RMSE = 0.81; top-7 predictors selected after %IncMSE; final model selected 7 factors.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Hong Kong the study leveraged sense of belonging to school and resilience (plus parents’ emotional support, teacher support, and perceived teacher interest) to predict positive affect, finding that school belonging was the most salient predictor and resilience was the second most influential. This indicates that interventions strengthening students’ school connectedness and coping/resilience may be effective levers for improving students’ day-to-day positive emotions, though the cross-sectional design prevents causal claims.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest regression with 10-fold cross-validation (5 repeats): R² = 14.47%, RMSE = 0.86; final model selected 7 factors; general fear of failure contributed 57.13%IncMSE and school belonging 31.38%IncMSE.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Hong Kong the study leveraged general fear of failure and school belonging (plus resilience, perceived cooperation, and teacher-directed instruction) to predict negative affect, finding that fear of failure was the top predictor and school belonging was the second most influential. This indicates that reducing evaluative pressure and fear of failure—while simultaneously improving students’ sense of belonging—may help mitigate negative emotions, though causality cannot be inferred from the predictive, cross-sectional models.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest regression with 10-fold cross-validation (5 repeats): R² = 19.83%, RMSE = 0.80; final model selected 7 factors; key predictors included school belonging, parental support, resilience, teacher support, and teacher interest with %IncMSE range 34.19 to 54.35.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Hong Kong the study leveraged school belonging and parental emotional support (along with resilience, teacher support, and teacher interest) to predict life satisfaction, finding that school belonging was among the strongest predictors and parental support also showed substantial importance. This indicates that family–school relational supports and supportive instructional climates may be promising targets for improving students’ global judgments of life satisfaction, while acknowledging that the study’s design is correlational.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest regression with 10-fold cross-validation (5 repeats): R² = 25.12%, RMSE = 0.75; final model selected 7 factors; top influential factors included resilience (ranked 1st), mastery goal orientation (ranked 3rd), work mastery (ranked 2nd), and school belonging; %IncMSE range 36.30 to 92.42.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Hong Kong the study leveraged resilience and mastery-related motivational factors (work mastery and mastery goal orientation, plus school belonging) to predict eudaimonic well-being (meaning in life), finding that resilience was the most influential predictor and mastery/work mastery were also key. This indicates that programs fostering students’ adaptive coping and mastery-oriented goal structures may strengthen students’ sense of purpose, though the cross-sectional evidence does not establish causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzed PISA 2018 Hong Kong student data (n = 6,037; grades 7–11) to predict two dimensions of subjective well-being (positive affect, negative affect, and life satisfaction) and one eudaimonic well-being construct (meaning in life). The authors first used random forest regression with 10-fold cross-validation (5 repeats) to rank predictors via %IncMSE and select a reduced set of key variables, then applied hierarchical linear modelling to account for the nested structure of students within schools. Predictive performance was moderate, with R² values of 19.15% (positive affect), 14.47% (negative affect), 19.83% (life satisfaction), and 25.12% (eudaimonic well-being), alongside RMSE values of 0.81, 0.86, 0.80, and 0.75 respectively. The most consistent top predictors were school belonging, parental emotional support, resilience, and mastery/fear-of-failure motivational factors. Limitations include the cross-sectional nature of PISA (no causal inference) and the lack of explicit reporting on whether PISA complex survey weights were applied.
